title: Your biggest customer wants a discount
text: The account that makes up a sixth of {city}’s revenue has sent procurement instead of the usual contact. They want 15% off, or they will "explore alternatives".

opts.label: Give the discount
opts.hint: Keep the account at a thinner margin.

out.text: They sign. The margin is gone but the volume stays.

opts.label: Offer a multi-year deal at 8% off
opts.hint: Trade price for commitment.

out.text: Three years, 8% off. Both sides can live with it.

opts.label: Refuse
opts.hint: Call the bluff.

out.text: They grumble and stay.
It was not a bluff.

lesson: Customer concentration is a risk you choose when you take the big account. Whoever needs the other less sets the price.

title: You are trending
text: A post about your product has been shared a few million times. The enquiries inbox is unusable.

opts.label: Pour fuel on it
opts.hint: Emergency marketing spend to turn attention into customers.

out.text: Two enormous quarters — if you can serve them.

opts.label: Enjoy it
opts.hint: Take what comes.

out.text: A pleasant bump.

opts.label: Use the moment to raise prices
opts.hint: Demand is hot. Charge for it.

out.text: Prices go up 5% and nobody blinks.

lesson: A demand spike is only worth what your capacity can serve. Check the limit on each office before spending to create demand you cannot meet.

title: A scathing review
text: An influential reviewer has taken your {city} operation apart, in detail, with screenshots.

opts.label: Respond and fix it
opts.hint: Admit the problems in public and spend to fix them.

out.text: The follow-up piece is headlined "They actually listened".
The fix is slow and the story lingers.

opts.label: Ignore it
opts.hint: It will blow over.

out.text: It does, eventually, after costing you customers.

opts.label: Send lawyers
opts.hint: It is defamatory. Probably.

out.text: The legal letter becomes the story.

lesson: Criticism you answer well can raise your reputation above where it started. Suppressing it reliably makes it louder.

title: A local competitor folds
text: One of the established names in {city} has closed its doors. Its customers need a new supplier this month.

opts.label: Hire their sales team
opts.hint: They know every customer by name.

out.text: Two of their best join, and bring their contacts.

opts.label: Buy the customer list
opts.hint: Pay the administrator for the contracts.

out.text: The accounts transfer to you.

opts.label: Let them come to you
opts.hint: Free is free.

out.text: Some find you on their own.

lesson: A competitor’s exit is the cheapest market share you will ever be offered — if you have the capacity to take the customers on.

title: A well-funded newcomer
text: A start-up with a famous investor and a large marketing budget has launched in {city}. They are giving the product away.

opts.label: Lock customers in
opts.hint: Offer long contracts at a small discount before they can be poached.

out.text: Most of your base signs for two years.

opts.label: Out-market them
opts.hint: Match their noise.

out.text: An expensive shouting match. You hold your ground.

opts.label: Ignore them
opts.hint: Free products run out of money.

out.text: They burn through their funding and fade.
They do not fade.

lesson: Entrants that buy share with investor money cannot do it for ever — but they can do it for longer than you might stay solvent matching them.

title: A customer goes bust
text: A significant customer has filed for bankruptcy. Their unpaid invoices are now a claim in a long queue.

opts.label: Write it off
opts.hint: Take the loss and move on.

out.text: The receivable is gone.

opts.label: Chase it through the courts
opts.hint: Legal fees for a place in the queue.

out.text: You recover a third.
Secured creditors take everything.

opts.label: Tighten credit for everyone
opts.hint: Deposits and shorter terms. Safer; some customers will walk.

out.text: Fewer sales, all of them collectable.

lesson: Revenue is not cash until it is collected. Every sale on credit is a small unsecured loan to your customer.

title: The platform raises its cut
text: The marketplace that brings you a third of your customers is raising its commission. Take it or leave it.

opts.label: Build direct sales
opts.hint: Spend to reach customers without the middleman.

out.text: A hard year, then freedom.

opts.label: Pass it on
opts.hint: Raise prices 4%.

out.text: Customers pay the platform’s tax.

opts.label: Absorb it
opts.hint: It is still cheaper than a sales force.

out.text: The margin shrinks.

lesson: If one channel controls your access to customers, your margin is theirs to take. Distribution you do not own is rented.

title: A free alternative
text: A capable open-source project now does most of what your product does. A large company is funding it.

opts.label: Open your core too
opts.hint: Give away the base, sell the enterprise layer.

out.text: Adoption jumps; price per customer falls.

opts.label: Go upmarket
opts.hint: Build what free software never does: compliance, support, integration.

out.text: The enterprise customers stay, and pay.

opts.label: Dismiss it
opts.hint: Serious customers do not run free software.

out.text: They do not, mostly.
They do.

lesson: When a substitute is free, you cannot compete on price. Compete on what the free option structurally cannot offer.

title: The industry gathers
text: The year’s main conference is next month. Your competitors have booked the big stands.

opts.label: Sponsor the keynote
opts.hint: Top billing.

out.text: Everyone who matters saw your name.

opts.label: Send a small team
opts.hint: Meet customers, skip the stand.

out.text: A handful of good conversations.

opts.label: Skip it
opts.hint: Nobody ever bought anything at a conference.

out.text: You save the money.

lesson: Marketing has diminishing returns. The first dollar of presence is worth a lot; the biggest stand in the hall mostly impresses other exhibitors.

title: Shortlisted
text: You are on the shortlist for the industry’s best-known award.

opts.label: Campaign for it
opts.hint: Dinners, a film, a table at the ceremony.

out.text: You win. The trophy goes in reception.
A rival wins. The dinner was nice.

opts.label: Let the work speak
opts.hint: Turn up and see.

out.text: You win anyway.
Not this year.

lesson: Recognition is a cheap brand asset when it comes — and a poor use of money when chased.

title: Renewals are slipping
text: More customers than usual are not renewing. Exit interviews mention reliability and slow support.

opts.label: Pause features, fix the basics
opts.hint: A quarter of engineering on reliability.

out.text: The complaints stop.

opts.label: Discount renewals
opts.hint: Buy them back.

out.text: They stay, at a lower price.

opts.label: Push on with the roadmap
opts.hint: New features will win them back.

out.text: They do not.

lesson: In a subscription business, churn compounds against you exactly as growth compounds for you. A leaky bucket cannot be filled by selling harder.

title: You are too cheap
text: A pricing consultant has benchmarked you against the market. Her conclusion: customers would pay 10% more and barely notice.

opts.label: Raise prices 10%
opts.hint: Believe the study.

out.text: The new price list is live. Watch your share over the next few quarters to see if she was right.

opts.label: Raise 4% and watch
opts.hint: A smaller step.

out.text: A cautious increase.

opts.label: Leave it
opts.hint: Share matters more than margin right now.

out.text: Prices stay where they are.

lesson: The right price depends on elasticity: how much volume you lose per point of price. Open any market-share number to see yours — and remember a price rise on idle capacity costs more than one on a full order book.

title: A reseller wants exclusivity
text: The largest distributor in {region} will push your product hard — if nobody else in the region can sell it.

opts.label: Sign the exclusive
opts.hint: Strong growth now; they become your only door.

out.text: Volume jumps.

opts.label: Offer non-exclusive
opts.hint: Less commitment on both sides.

out.text: They take it, with less enthusiasm.

opts.label: Decline
opts.hint: Keep control of your channel.

out.text: You keep selling direct.

lesson: Exclusivity trades growth for dependence. The partner who controls your access to customers will eventually price that control.

title: Your reseller wants better terms
text: Your exclusive distributor in {region} now accounts for most of your sales there. They would like a larger margin.

opts.label: Give in
opts.hint: They have you.

out.text: The margin moves from your account to theirs.

opts.label: Walk away
opts.hint: Rebuild the channel yourself.

out.text: A painful year in the region.

lesson: This is what dependence costs. The time to negotiate was before they controlled the channel.

title: An enterprise pilot
text: One of the largest companies in {region} wants to roll your product out to forty thousand seats — if you build six features only they need.

opts.label: Build what they ask
opts.hint: A quarter of engineering on one customer. Big account, a product that bends to it.

out.text: They sign a three-year deal and tell their peers.
Their procurement team stalls for a year, then picks a rival anyway.

opts.label: Offer the standard product
opts.hint: Say no to custom work; they may still buy.

out.text: They buy it as it is.
They go elsewhere.

opts.label: Decline politely
opts.hint: Protect the roadmap.

out.text: You stay focused.

lesson: Big customers are worth a lot and cost more than they appear: custom work becomes permanent maintenance. Price it in before you say yes.

title: Charge by usage?
text: Your head of product wants to switch from per-seat to usage-based pricing. Small customers would pay less; heavy users much more.

opts.label: Switch
opts.hint: Wider adoption, lumpier revenue.

out.text: Adoption jumps and the heavy users pay up.
Heavy users optimise their usage and your revenue dips.

opts.label: Keep per-seat
opts.hint: Predictable, if dull.

out.text: Nothing changes.

lesson: Pricing model is strategy: it decides which customers you attract and how revenue scales with the value you deliver.

title: Every customer wants an AI assistant
text: Three of your top ten customers asked about AI features this month. Two rivals have announced theirs.

opts.label: Build it properly
opts.hint: Two quarters of your best engineers, plus inference costs.

out.text: It works and customers love it.
It demos well and disappoints in use.

opts.label: Partner with a model provider
opts.hint: Faster and cheaper; they keep the data advantage.

out.text: A decent feature in a quarter.

opts.label: Wait for the hype to settle
opts.hint: Most AI features are demos.

out.text: Customers lose interest.
Customers do not lose interest.

lesson: Features that every competitor can buy from the same supplier do not differentiate for long. Ask what you can build that they cannot.

title: The delivery apps want a cut
text: The two big delivery apps say a third of your customers now order through them. They want 30% commission.

opts.label: List on both apps
opts.hint: More orders at a much thinner margin.

out.text: Orders climb; margins fall.

opts.label: Build your own ordering
opts.hint: Expensive, but the customer relationship stays yours.

out.text: Fewer orders at first, but you keep the margin.

opts.label: Stay off the apps
opts.hint: Your customers will come to you.

out.text: Some will. Some will not.

lesson: Aggregators own the demand and rent it back to you. The more customers they control, the more of your margin they can take.

title: A dish goes viral
text: A video of one of your dishes in {city} has twenty million views. The queue is around the block.

opts.label: Extend hours and hire temps
opts.hint: Serve the queue while it lasts.

out.text: Two extraordinary quarters.

opts.label: Raise the price of the dish
opts.hint: Let the queue pay for itself.

out.text: People pay it.

lesson: A demand spike is only worth what you can serve. Temporary capacity is expensive, but turning customers away is free advertising for your rivals.

title: The automaker wants more
text: Your biggest customer is demanding another 8% off and faster delivery, or it moves the contract.

opts.label: Concede
opts.hint: Keep the volume.

out.text: Margins on the contract go to almost nothing.

opts.label: Refuse
opts.hint: Lose the contract.

out.text: A third of your volume disappears.

lesson: Customer concentration hands pricing power to the customer.

title: The client will not pay
text: A client says your last project did not deliver what was promised and will not pay the final invoice.

opts.label: Negotiate a discount
opts.hint: Get most of it.

out.text: You settle at 70%.

opts.label: Redo the work for free
opts.hint: Make it right.

out.text: Costly, and the client stays.

opts.label: Sue
opts.hint: The contract is clear.

out.text: You win and lose the client.
You lose and lose the client.

lesson: Scope creep and vague promises turn into bad debts. Clear contracts are a working-capital tool.

title: A generic challenge
text: A generics manufacturer has challenged one of your patents, aiming to launch a copy before expiry.

opts.label: Defend the patent
opts.hint: Years of litigation.

out.text: The patent holds.
The patent falls. Prices collapse.

opts.label: Settle and license
opts.hint: Let them launch later, for a fee.

out.text: A delayed generic and a royalty.

lesson: Patent protection is the value of a drug. When it ends, the price can fall by 80% within a year.

title: Downgraded
text: The most-followed analyst on your stock has cut it to "sell", citing slowing growth.

opts.label: Hold an investor day
opts.hint: Lay out the next five years.

out.text: The market buys the story.
The story does not land.

opts.label: Let the results speak
opts.hint: One quarter at a time.

out.text: The shares fall and wait for evidence.

lesson: Share prices move on expectations. A public company manages them whether it means to or not.

title: Shareholders want a dividend
text: Your largest shareholders say the cash pile is "lazy" and want a regular dividend.

opts.label: Start a dividend
opts.hint: A steady payout signals confidence; cutting it later will hurt.

out.text: A dividend is declared.

opts.label: Explain your plans for the cash
opts.hint: Growth is a better use.

out.text: They accept, if the growth comes.
They are not convinced.

lesson: Cash not invested at a good return belongs to the shareholders. A dividend is a commitment the market will hold you to.
